newsitem.title: USA: Fla. judge's tobacco ruling turns tables on state.
newsitem.headline: Fla. judge's tobacco ruling turns tables on state.

text.p: Evidence that the state of Florida made and distributed cigarettes to prisoners can be used by tobacco companies defending against a lawsuit seeking damages for the public cost of smoking-related illness, a judge ruled Thursday.
The decision by Circuit Judge Harold Cohen means the state would have to accept a share of any damages awarded by the jury in the trial, which is scheduled to begin on August 4.
"It could cost Florida millions of dollars if the jury ever gets this case," attorney Stephen Krigbaum, who represents Philip Morris Cos, said.
Florida sued the cigarette makers, including Philip Morris and RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, to recoup taxpayer money spent treating tobacco-related illnesses.
The tobacco companies contend Florida also made cigarettes and distributed them to prison inmates in the 1920s and continued to do so until the early 1970s.
Because of that, the tobacco companies asked Cohen to include the state corrections department and other agencies as parties to the lawsuit the state filed against the cigarette makers.
Attorney Jose Martinez, who represents Dosal Tobacco Co. of Opa-locka, Florida, said that in one year alone, the state distributed 4.5 million of its own manufactured cigarettes.
"I believe I am entitled to say if I did it (made a harmful product), you did worse," Martinez said of the state.
He said Dosal did not begin supplying the state with cigarettes until after Florida stopped making them.

Wayne Hogan, one of the attorneys representing Florida in the lawsuit, argued there was no need to include the corrections department or other state agencies in the case because Florida was only seeking damages for smoking-related illnesses from 1994 through 1996, long after the state stopped making tobacco products.

Even if Florida did manufacture unsafe cigarettes, Assistant Attorney General Gerald Curington argued that Florida could not be held accountable because it has sovereign immunity from lawsuits. Curington also said any state "planning-level decisions" on the manufacture of cigarettes were beyond the authority of the court to review.

Cohen agreed that the tobacco companies could not raise the state's manufacture of cigarettes as an actual defense of their own actions. But the judge said, cigarette companies do have the right to introduce facts that could help reduce their share of any damage award granted in the trial.
